generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, active engagement is the difference between a reader who accepts a textbook's summary of an effect and one who asks what evidence it rests on. A settled-sounding claim, that a therapy 'works', say, invites an active reader to ask how it was tested, in whom, and against what comparison. Opening up that discourse, rather than taking the summary as final, is the everyday habit of a critical psychologist.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students read the same textbook passage, which states a well-known effect as though it were settled.

Tom reads it, accepts the effect, and writes it into his notes as a fact. The point is captured, but Tom has taken the textbook's word for it, with no sense of the studies behind the claim or the debate around it. This is passive engagement.

Amara pauses on the word that makes it sound settled. Is this really agreed? She checks what the claim rests on, finds the original studies and a recent failure to replicate, and sees the field is still arguing. The effect goes into her notes as a position to weigh, not a fact to repeat. This is active engagement: she has opened up the discourse.

Both read the passage. Only Amara treated it as something to question.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, being critical becomes real work when you engage with a source actively: questioning its claim, checking the evidence, and bringing in other studies rather than accepting a single summary. You can now tell active engagement from passive and choose an active move when a claim sounds settled. The next lesson gives you the language to describe these moves.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that opened up the discourse around the source?

items.text: She found the original studies and a failed replication, and saw the field was still arguing.
She accepted the effect because the textbook stated it clearly.
She read the passage more slowly than Tom did.
She copied the claim into her notes word for word.

feedback.correct: That's right. Bringing in the original studies and a failed replication turned a single claim into a live debate.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that brought in other evidence or views, rather than accepting or copying the claim.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara opened up the discourse by finding the original studies and a failed replication. Accepting, re-reading or copying all leave the single claim as the last word.
